column2: Read permits reading, not modifying or deleting; other options each deny reading or grant unrelated administration. Textbook Windows share-permission context, not a universal filesystem ACL claim.
Read/Write grants reading and modification within assigned scope; it does not disable security, modify passwords or open accounts elsewhere. Qualified scope makes the key precise.
Discovery advertises/discovers network devices; it is not a password reset, uninstall or power-control mechanism. Does not by itself grant access rights.
Correct Add operation in the textbook's Windows Specific people sharing dialog; clarify this UI context so the instruction is not presented as universal across OS versions.
Clearing Share this folder disables the Advanced Sharing share; naming folders, printer queues and wallpaper settings cannot do so.

The Private network profile is appropriate for a trusted local network; anonymous advertisers, spam and airport strangers are not trusted users. Does not imply encryption is guaranteed by profile choice.
Print serving receives/spools jobs and controls printer access; it does not translate documents, allocate Internet addresses or erase all files.
Sharing is the correct Printer properties tab for the described Windows UI. Distractors deliberately mismatch Security/General/Ports with non-tab functions.
Excessive sharing increases exposure and modification risk; unrelated port count, brightness and printer-speed claims cannot explain the risk. Basic TH reasoning.
Sharing/discovery/permissions are relevant checks after physical connection; display/print/cooling settings are not. Does not claim these are the only possible connectivity causes.
Pooling one physical printer can reduce equipment and manual transfers; other choices require extra hardware or assert unrelated automatic capacity/erasure. Sound TH rationale.
Network video class is online communication; face-to-face conversation and paper media are not. No ambiguity from reading paper together without network use.
Remote communication with connectivity is an advantage; identity authenticity, equipment-free operation and invisible facial cues are not guaranteed.
Replacing travel directly reduces travel time/cost; printer ink, storage size and switch ports are not the primary saving described.
Plain text lacks live facial/voice cues; text can be stored, transmit characters and reach remote people, so the other omissions are false.
Personal-data disclosure/misuse is a privacy risk; shorter journeys, wider networks and tool choice are advantages, not the requested risk.
Connectivity/software failure can interrupt a meeting; supportive, polite listening behaviors do not describe technical interruption causes.
Connecting geographically separated people with shared interests expands social links; same-room restrictions contradict the online benefit.
Email and video conferencing are network communication tools; paper letters, chalkboards and stationery are not. NB distinction within lesson6.
The four humanistic principles match the book: respect, courtesy, empathy, support. All distractors are harmful behaviors, therefore easy but not multi-key.
Keeping private messages confidential absent permission exemplifies ordinary respectful communication; ignoring help, not reading or refusing to listen do not.
Evidence-based, appropriate language is courteous disagreement; mockery, threats and abusive personal attacks are not justified rebuttal.
Perspective-taking is empathy; fabricating accusations or exploiting private images contradicts it.
Encouragement and useful assistance are support; shaming, disclosure and agitation harm the recipient instead.
Verify truth and privacy before sharing; title-only, likes-only and sensationalism-only checks cannot establish accuracy or consent.
Reading carefully and responding respectfully is appropriate disagreement; doxxing, threats and author insults are not.
Reflection and adjustment improve conduct; suppressing all opposing evidence, disclosing secrets or ignoring sound feedback do not.
Appropriate attire/background is a suitable video-call courtesy; deliberately offensive presentation and aggressive speech are not. No intrusive camera-permission implication.
Pseudonymity/impersonation can obstruct identity assessment; universal verified-name or same-room claims are false.
Diverse tools enable a suitable mode for a communication need; they neither remove privacy protections nor guarantee fault-free links.
Remote participation reduces geographic constraints provided devices/connectivity exist; the rationale appropriately retains those prerequisites.
Key/rationale correct only without permission. Add that explicit premise to the diary-sharing stem; authorized sharing is not necessarily a privacy violation.
Critiquing reasoning instead of the person protects respectful dialogue; other choices endorse hostility or evasion of verification.
Correct aim is avoiding misunderstanding/escalation, not abandoning all communication. Polish awkward 'kích thích đối phương' to a clear de-escalation phrase without changing key.
Emotional encouragement can be support; exposure, isolation and criticism are harm rather than benefit. TH is intentionally basic.
Unverified allegation calls for verification/non-amplification, not coercion or more distribution. Applied ethics key unique, but easy VD rather than a calibrated difficult item.
Explain and encourage a confused learner; shaming/removal/disclosure defeats support. Simple scenario application aligned with lesson6.
False: a closed group is still third-party disclosure and does not replace the diary owner's permission.
True: discouraging further spread protects the affected person's privacy and dignity.
True: stop redistributing and support Hoa's response; both parts mitigate the stated harm.
False: publishing complete diary/name further exposes Hoa; supportive intent cannot make this remedial action appropriate.
True: respectful, non-personal wording is necessary to the described courteous disagreement.
False: disagreement over a solution does not license attacks on the writer's dignity.
True: reading fully and supplying specific reasons applies evidence-based, calm rebuttal instead of threats.
False: ridicule is harmful and does not establish understanding or a safe learning environment.
False: sharing interests does not authenticate identity; impersonation/pseudonyms remain possible.
True: requested home address and identity documents are sensitive and may create privacy risks.
False: unknown identity plus unnecessary document demand gives no sound basis for immediate disclosure.
True: withholding data and seeking a trusted person's support is appropriate, not a guarantee every unknown account is malicious.
True: unverified reputation allegations can harm others even if a sharer did not originate them.
False: popularity/likes are not verification of each factual claim.
True: checking original source and delaying doubtful sharing applies the lesson's accuracy/privacy obligations.
False: adding insults amplifies harm rather than demonstrating humanistic conduct.
False: humiliating someone for asking contradicts empathy and support.
True: genuine encouragement can make the learner feel supported; the qualified 'can' is accurate.
False: publishing distress images to force confidence may violate privacy and intensify harm.
True: clear explanations, courtesy and encouragement address both confusion and fear in the given group.
body contains the displayed document body, unlike head/title metadata and style rules; no CSS requirement is implied.
title in head sets the document title typically shown in the browser tab; meta/body/html-inside-title are not equivalent markup.
HTML doctype identifies HTML/standards parsing, not password, DNS or CSS; it is a declaration rather than a content element.
Notepad++ edits source text with syntax support; graphics viewers/recorders are not source editors in the named options.
br is a void line-break element; it does not title the tab, create a table or embed audio.
Only <!-- ... --> is ordinary HTML comment syntax; comments are not rendered paragraph text, although source remains inspectable.
html is the document element; head/body are its children and meta is void, not a root container. Valid-source scope makes the key unique.
charset identifies character encoding (UTF-8), not font, dimensions or an audio URL. Encoding declaration does not itself transcode incorrectly saved bytes.
HTML source is text, allowing a plain-text editor; it is not stored inherently as compressed image, sound or a radio signal.
Explicit snippet places CLB in title and Chào in body; CLB becomes tab/document title rather than body text. Matches browser-semantics test.
img is void and must not have an end tag; alternative location/root restrictions are false.
True: img is a void element without a corresponding end tag in HTML syntax.
False: ordinary HTML comments are not rendered as paragraph content; source accessibility does not contradict this.
True: a UTF-8 meta declaration is appropriate for this UTF-8 file; this is a recommendation, not a claim every undeclared document always decodes incorrectly.
False: changing an image width cannot fix document text character decoding.
HTML has six heading ranks h1–h6; p1/t1/b1 series do not define heading ranks.
strong conveys importance/seriousness, usually bold, whereas strike/select/source are not the requested strong markup. Very easy stem names the tag; no claim bold alone is semantics.
sub represents subscript; sup is superscript and sum/src are not the corresponding HTML text elements.
style accepts inline CSS declarations; class selects a class, title is advisory metadata and start is not an inline-style container.
font-family sets the font family, not weight/style/size; rationale distinguishes all three distractors precisely.
x<sup>2</sup> is the superscript representation; sub, del and ins express different semantics.
Attributes are written in start tags; end tags, filenames and external browser chrome are not attribute-declaration locations.
hr is a thematic break often drawn horizontally; not italic text, number input or audio. Explanation correctly separates semantics from default rendering.
Defaults matter: span is inline, p block; CSS can override display but stem explicitly excludes that ambiguity by asking the default.
CSS color sets foreground text color in the supplied paragraph; background/border/filename require other mechanisms.
Semicolons delimit CSS declarations, unlike ?, / or !. Final semicolon is optional but the requested separator is still unique.
True: h1–h6 encode heading hierarchy, not merely six arbitrary visual sizes.
False: span is inline by default and is not a paragraph-sized independent block.
False: semantic emphasis/importance can be marked with em/strong without rasterizing the entire article.
True: p represents a paragraph, addressing separate paragraph content; it does not promise print pagination.
